overview: United Energy Group (UEG) is a Hong Kong-listed independent upstream oil and gas company with producing assets concentrated in Pakistan, Iraq (via its Kuwait Energy subsidiary's Block 9 and Siba interests) and, since October 2025, an enlarged Egypt position following the acquisition of Apex International Energy's Western Desert concessions. The Group is principally engaged in upstream exploration and production, an energy/commodities trading business, and a small but growing clean energy segment (wind, solar, BESS). It describes itself as one of the largest listed integrated energy companies in Hong Kong, with a reserve life exceeding 15 years and 2P working-interest reserves of roughly 680 mmboe at end-2025.

business_model.summary: Revenue is generated from (1) sale of crude oil, condensate, LPG and natural gas produced from working interests in Pakistan, Iraq and Egypt, priced off Brent crude (with PSC-based discounts in Egypt and government off-take in Pakistan/Iraq), and (2) a trading business that lifts and resells equity crude/products and third-party energy commodities with international counterparties (BP, Total, Trafigura, Aramco, Itochu, PTT, etc.). A small clean-energy segment (a 99MW wind farm in Pakistan under a long-term PPA with the state Central Power Purchase Agency, plus an off-grid solar/BESS installation in Iraq and early-stage European solar/BESS projects) contributes modestly to turnover but is a stated strategic priority. E&P revenue is essentially commodity-price- and volume-driven (not recurring/subscription in nature); trading revenue is largely pass-through/volume-driven with thin margins. FY2025 turnover mix: Exploration & Production ~49%, Trading ~50%, Clean energy ~1% (trading share has grown materially, partly reflecting higher throughput rather than higher-margin activity).
business_model.customer_type: B2B/B2G — government-owned gas distributors and national oil companies (Sui Southern Gas Co. in Pakistan, Basra Oil Company and EGPC for Iraq/Egypt crude off-take) plus international oil majors and trading houses
business_model.geographic_mix: Upstream assets in Pakistan (20 blocks, largest foreign E&P footprint in the country), Iraq (60% of EDPSC Block 9, 30% of Siba/GDPSC, 100% of FAO exploration block), and Egypt (11 blocks post-Apex, Western/Eastern Desert); corporate base in Hong Kong with reported business presence extending to MENA and Europe (clean energy).

main_competitors: Kuwait Energy's regional MENA peers and other Iraq/Kurdistan IOCs (e.g., Gulf Keystone Petroleum, ShaMaran Petroleum, Genel Energy)
Pakistan E&P incumbents (Oil & Gas Development Company (OGDC), Mari Petroleum, Pakistan Petroleum Limited, Pakistan Oilfields)
Egypt Western Desert operators (Apache/APA Corporation, Cheiron Petroleum, Dana Gas, Kuwait Energy's own former Egyptian JVs)
Other Hong Kong/China-linked internationally focused upstream players (e.g., CNOOC, Sinopec's overseas units) competing for MENA/South Asia licenses and M&A targets
competitive_position.market_position: Self-described as the largest foreign oil and gas E&P company operating in Pakistan by acreage, and (post-Apex) among the top five international oil producers in Egypt; a mid-tier operator in Iraq's Basra province where it operates Block 9 (national ambition to lift output toward 100,000 b/d). Not a major global player by production scale (~160-200 kboed gross), but a relevant niche operator in each of its three core countries.

moat_factors.description: Operator status on most of its blocks (Block 9, Siba, FAO, most Pakistan and Egypt licenses) gives control over pace/cost of development; reserve life >15 years provides long visibility, though reserves are depleting assets rather than a renewable moat.

moat_factors.factor: Incumbency and local expertise in Pakistan
moat_factors.description: Decades of operating history and the largest foreign E&P footprint in Pakistan (~27,600 km²) create regulatory relationships and sub-surface knowledge that are difficult for new entrants to replicate quickly.
Management repeatedly cites an 'industry-leading low-cost advantage' (operating expenses of roughly US$4-8/boe across its assets), supporting margin resilience in weak price environments.
Long-term gas sales agreements with state-owned buyers (Sui Southern Gas, BOC) provide demand certainty but also concentrate counterparty/payment risk with sovereign entities.
No meaningful brand or network-effect moat; this is a commodity-production business where differentiation is mainly operational execution and asset quality.

weaknesses: No pricing power — a price-taker on Brent-linked crude and negotiated gas contracts
Geographic concentration in politically volatile jurisdictions (Pakistan, Iraq, Egypt) with history of production curtailments beyond the company's control
Trading segment carries thin, commodity-exposed margins and growing share of a lower-quality revenue mix
Governance overhang from controlling shareholder's regulatory history (see Recent Developments) and a complex, multi-layered offshore ownership structure
Reliance on third-party reserve auditors and PSC/concession renewal risk in each jurisdiction

growth_drivers: Egypt expansion via the Apex International Energy acquisition (completed 14 October 2025, ~US$150-158m), adding 11 blocks and lifting the Group into the top five international oil producers in Egypt; working-interest production from Egypt grew ~87-97% YoY in H1 2026

Iraq Block 9 production ramp-up, underpinned by completion of a 72km gas/LPG flowline and a new Central Processing Facility (gas/LPG sales began June 2025); government ambition for Block 9 output to reach ~100,000 b/d
Continued exploration success in Pakistan (new Sawan South, Kalchas South and Kuhan blocks; 2P reserve additions) and in Egypt (Apex-area discoveries)
Iraq FAO exploration block (100% interest) — first well delivered a commercial discovery in 2025 with appraisal ongoing
Clean energy diversification — European solar/BESS projects progressing toward commercial terms, and MENA framework agreements (Egypt, Morocco, Jordan, Mauritania) for future renewables development
Prudent/low leverage balance sheet (gearing ratio ~12-15%) gives optionality for further debt-funded or equity-funded M&A, and management has flagged possible international bond issuance
Favorable long-term Pakistan gas supply/demand gap (declining domestic production vs. rising demand) effectively guarantees offtake for the Group's predominantly gas production there

business.description: Iraq's Block 9 and Siba production were curtailed by Basra Oil Company directives during the H1 2026 Strait of Hormuz crisis, with gross production down >20% at times; such interruptions can recur with any renewed regional conflict.
Mature Pakistan fields are in decline (2025 Pakistan output down ~16% YoY); sustained production depends on continued exploration success and new licenses/acquisitions.

FY2023 saw working-interest 2P reserves in Iraq fall ~33% YoY alongside a swing to a reported net loss; oil & gas assets carry impairment risk tied to price decks and reserve re-certification (FY2025 again booked ~HK$416m of net impairment and ~HK$210m of dry-well write-offs).
Key gas customers are state-owned entities (Sui Southern Gas Co., Basra Oil Company) and crude is sold to Egypt's EGPC under PSC terms — concentrated counterparty and sovereign payment risk.

financial.description: Weighted average interest rate on borrowings rose to ~9.9% at H1 2026 (from ~9.7% in H1 2025); all borrowings are USD-denominated term loans, making finance costs sensitive to global rates and the company's credit spread (Fitch BB-/S&P B+).
H1 2026 operating cash flow was roughly flat YoY despite higher profit, partly due to an increase in trade receivables; an allowance for trade receivables of HK$120m was also booked in H1 2026.
Board has not recommended an interim dividend; capital is being retained for capex/M&A, which may not suit income-oriented investors.

regulatory.description: Former Chairman Zhang Hong Wei was fined and handed a lifetime securities-market ban by the CSRC (China Securities Regulatory Commission) in 2025 over disclosure violations at an affiliated company (Orient Group), triggering his resignation as Chairman/executive director in June 2025; related entities (He Fu International, Ace Victory) show a charging order on a ~13.8% equity stake as of April 2026, creating an ownership/governance overhang.

regulatory.risk: Vacant CEO role / governance code deviation
regulatory.description: The Company discloses non-compliance with CG Code provision C.2.1 as the Chief Executive Officer post remains vacant, with executive duties performed collectively by the Board.

regulatory.risk: Production-sharing contract and concession renewal/fiscal terms
regulatory.description: Operations depend on PSC/concession agreements with Pakistan, Iraqi (BOC) and Egyptian (EGPC) state authorities; fiscal terms, royalty/windfall levies and contract renewals are government-controlled and can change (Egypt has been actively revising fiscal incentives, a tailwind for now but a reminder of discretion).

Operating in Iraq and the broader Middle East exposes the Group to sanctions regimes, conflict-related force majeure declarations, and shipping-route disruption (Strait of Hormuz) outside management's control.

macro.description: Revenue and profit are highly sensitive to Brent crude prices, which swung from ~US$65/bbl to ~US$120/bbl and back to ~US$75/bbl within H1 2026 alone due to the US-Iran conflict; average realized oil price directly drives E&P turnover and margins.

The 2026 US-Iran conflict and Strait of Hormuz disruption directly curtailed Iraq Assets' production and lifting; Egypt and Pakistan assets partially offset this but regional escalation remains a persistent tail risk given reserve concentration in MENA/South Asia.

Reporting currency is HKD (pegged to USD) and most transactions/borrowings are USD-denominated, limiting translation risk; some exposure to RMB, Pakistani Rupee, Iraqi Dinar and Egyptian Pound is described as not significant, and the Group does not hedge currency exposure.

Long-term decarbonization trends could pressure hydrocarbon demand and financing availability, though near-to-medium-term IEA/OPEC demand forecasts still show growth, and the Group is hedging this risk via its own clean-energy diversification.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: OPEC's July 2026 Monthly Oil Market Report projected global oil demand growth of 0.8 mmbbld in 2026 to ~105.94 mmbbld, driven mainly by non-OECD economies, with OPEC+ unwinding voluntary production cuts; the IMF projected global growth slowing to 3.0% in 2026 (from Middle East conflict effects) before rebounding to 3.4% in 2027, with inflation rising to 4.7% in 2026.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High — upstream E&P earnings are directly geared to Brent oil prices and production volumes, both of which are subject to macro, OPEC+ policy and geopolitical swings; FY2023 and FY2025 both saw material swings in profitability tied to price and impairment cycles.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate — all borrowings are USD-denominated floating/term loans (weighted average rate ~9.8-9.9%), so global USD rate levels and the Group's own credit spread affect finance costs, though gearing is low (~12-15%) limiting absolute exposure.
key_input_costs: Diesel/power costs at remote field sites (partially mitigated by grid connection and solar/BESS investments in Egypt and Iraq)
Government royalties, windfall levies and 'government take' on produced volumes

recent_developments.event: Completed acquisition of Apex International Energy Holdings I's Egyptian upstream business (~US$150-158m), adding 11 Western Desert blocks and lifting the Group into the top five international oil producers in Egypt.

Chairman and executive director Zhang Hong Wei resigned following a CSRC fine and lifetime securities-market ban related to disclosure violations at affiliated Orient Group; Song Yu was re-designated Chairman and Chiu Ping Shun appointed as an additional executive director.
Fitch Ratings assigned the Group a long-term issuer rating of 'BB-' with stable outlook, following S&P's earlier 'B+' stable rating — both sub-investment grade but validating financial resilience.
Voluntary Q4 2025 operational update filed, reporting continued production ramp-up ahead of FY2025 results.

US-Iran conflict and closure/restriction of the Strait of Hormuz forced Basra Oil Company (BOC) to impose production curtailments on the Group's Iraq Assets (Block 9 and Siba); curtailments were fully lifted in early June 2026 and Iraq production has recovered to pre-conflict levels, while Brent crude spiked to ~US$120/bbl in March before easing to ~US$75/bbl by end-June.

Ace Victory Developments Limited was granted a charging order against ~13.85% of the Company's shares held by He Fu International Limited (linked to former chairman Zhang Hong Wei's family office structure), adding an overhang/uncertainty to the register of substantial shareholders.
MSCI upgraded the Group's ESG rating to AA, placing it in the top quartile of its peer group.

H1 2026 interim results: turnover up 33.7% YoY to HK$10.94bn and net profit up 28.7% YoY to HK$952.7m, driven by higher realized Brent-linked prices and a larger trading book, despite a 14% YoY decline in gross production caused by the Iraq curtailments.

items.notes: Narrowed/lowered from the 179,000-213,000 boed range given at FY2025 results (March 2026), reflecting the Strait of Hormuz-related curtailments experienced in H1 2026.
Down from the 105,400-125,300 boed range given in the FY2025 annual report; Pakistan guided at 24,600-27,100 boed, Iraq at 61,000-68,400 boed, Egypt at 19,800-23,400 boed.

Tightened from the US$500-650 million range guided at FY2025 results and down from ~US$750 million actually spent in 2025; management says it will aim for the lower end of the range given Strait of Hormuz uncertainty.

items.target: Maintain low gearing, explore international debt capital markets including a possible corporate bond
items.notes: Gearing ratio was 12.1% at 30 June 2026 (down from 15.3% at FY2025 year-end); management continues to flag capital-structure optimization and potential bond issuance to fund organic and inorganic growth.

guidance.management_commentary: Management stated it 'remains confident of delivering solid operational and financial performance for 2026' as Strait of Hormuz transit normalizes and Iraq Assets' oil lifting returns to pre-disruption levels, even though the resumption of supply routes may put some downward pressure on oil prices (still elevated versus 2025 averages). The Board did not recommend an interim dividend for H1 2026, prioritizing cash retention for development capex and balance-sheet flexibility.

bull_case: Diversified three-country asset base (Pakistan, Iraq, Egypt) demonstrated resilience during the 2026 Middle East conflict — Egypt and Pakistan assets partly offset Iraq curtailments, and Iraq output has since fully recovered

Low leverage (gearing ~12%) and strong gearing/interest-coverage profile versus most E&P peers, with two sub-investment-grade but stable credit ratings (Fitch BB-, S&P B+) supporting access to capital for further bolt-on M&A
Egypt platform meaningfully scaled via the Apex acquisition, now a top-five international producer in-country with further integration/production upside still to be realized
Long reserve life (>15 years) and multiple ongoing exploration successes (10+ commercial discoveries across FY2025/H1 2026) support multi-year production visibility without needing further M&A
Trades at a low reported P/E (~8x per most recent screen) versus the broader market, with industry-leading low-cost operations supporting margin resilience even in a lower oil-price environment
bear_case: Revenue and earnings are highly levered to volatile, geopolitically-driven Brent oil prices and to production volumes that can be abruptly curtailed by host-government directives (as seen with BOC's Iraq curtailments in H1 2026)

Governance overhang from former Chairman Zhang Hong Wei's CSRC fine/lifetime ban and the subsequent charging order against ~13.85% of shares held by an affiliated entity, raising questions about shareholder-register stability and related-party history

Concentrated operations in politically sensitive jurisdictions (Pakistan, Iraq, Egypt) exposed to sanctions risk, shipping-route disruptions (Strait of Hormuz), and sovereign counterparty/payment risk on gas and crude offtake agreements

History of sizable non-cash impairments and dry-well write-offs (FY2023 net loss, FY2025 ~HK$416m of net impairments) tied to reserve re-certification, which can obscure underlying cash generation and create earnings volatility
No dividend currently paid and CEO role structurally vacant (CG Code non-compliance), which may deter income-focused or governance-sensitive investors despite strong operating cash flow
